units.translation: “of the youths.” We often say “they are younger” instead of “young,” and in the poet (Iliad 14.137) “he took her right hand” instead of “right.”
b. “had been toiled”: the word “quickly” is used with “had been toiled” to indicate the eagerness and speed of the young men, as if they were actively making, preparing.
264-65a. “prey” means something taken up, plunder; or food. “Last” means final. The word “rushing” is used for the dense flight of the Harpies.
b. “unexpected” either instead of “unforeseen” or instead of “bitter”; for “deukos” means sweet. P
268-69a. “unforeseen”: instead of “unforeseen,” “without pretext,” as if without pretext and delay and postponement, since postponement accompanies those who make pretexts.

b. “raging with a shriek”: they rushed with a shriek, desiring food. This is said as of birds of prey; for those also like to shriek before seizing. And “they rushed” refers to their dense swooping and speed.
b. “over the sea”: that they pursued them through the Aegean and Sicilian seas, Pherecydes says in the sixth book (FGrHist 3 F 28 J.).
274. “holding swords”: holding their swords in their hands, they ran similarly behind them. L
275. “but they would not have followed without Zeus”: for, he says, they would not have followed the Harpies apart from Zeus.

276-77a. “since of the west wind”: either they ran swifter than the blasts of the southwest wind or equal to the blasts, as Hesiod says (Theogony 268). Since the Harpies always flew past even the gusts of the west wind, whenever they came to Phineus' house or withdrew from there.

b. The whirlings of storm winds are swifter than breezes. For it happens that a breeze is stretched out and lingers, but a storm wind is swifter and lighter than a breeze. And reasonably so; for the west wind is the swiftest of the other winds, as Homer also says (Iliad 19.415-16): “we two could run with the breath of the west wind, which they say is the lightest.”

279a. “or tracking deer”: some animal similar to a deer, the so-called fawn. Dionysius the Athenian says in his Foundations (FGrHist 12 F 12 M. IV 395) that deer are called “prokes”; whence also Proconnesus, since deer abound in it. Others say Prochonnesus is named from the water-pitcher which Parthenos had when she met the Milesians as they were sending out the colony. Others etymologize Prochonnesus, in that formerly being an island it was later joined by silting. By some Proconnesus was also called Elaphonesus. Philetas (fr. 48 Kuchenm.) says that deer that give birth for the first time are called “prokes,” as it were first-born.
b. “stretching a little”: they ran a little apart with a gap.
